newsitem.title: USA: Europeans to join Korean nuclear group.
newsitem.headline: Europeans to join Korean nuclear group.

text.p: The European Union, carrying strong political and financial support, would within months become a member of the international consortium working with North Korea to dismantle Pyongyang's nuclear program, the head of the project said on Wednesday.

Stephen Bosworth of the Korean Energy Development Organization (KEDO) also told reporters the group was fully re-engaged with the communist North Korean government after it apologized in December for one of its submarines infiltrating South Korea last September.

He said however, that the consortium -- led by the United States, South Korea and Japan -- was still having difficulty raising money to buy heavy fuel oil it promised North Korea as part of the 1994 Geneva agreement signed by Washington and Pyongyang.

"This (EU membership) is a very important development, not only in terms of its help on our financial problem but much more fundamentally in terms of the political weight that European Union membership gives this organization," Bosworth said in a telephone news conference.

He said the European Union would become an executive board member along with the current three leading countries when it joins "in a few months" time. General members of KEDO are Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Indonesia, Finland, Argentina and Chile.

Under the $4.5 billion deal, Washington promised the isolationist state two light-water reactors generating 1,000 megawatts of power each by approximately 2003 if Pyongyang froze and ultimately dismantled its existing nuclear program. North Korea was assured interim energy in the form of 500,000 metric tons of heavy fuel oil per year for heating and electricity.
Light-water reactors are less suitable for producing weapons-grade plutonium than the graphite-moderated reactors built by North Korea.

"We did continue to ship heavy fuel oil to North Korea even during the pause in the project and we met fully our commitment for 1996 with some difficulty," said Bosworth, executive director of KEDO. "Financing remains a very serious problem in that program. We had to go out and in effect borrow to finance heavy fuel oil purchases."
He said KEDO's combination of debt for heavy fuel oil, including a $19 million special credit facility from Japan, was about $35 million. The overall estimated cost of the project is not yet known.
Bosworth said the North Koreans had been "very positive and businesslike" and he saw no change in their attitude toward the nuclear project since the submarine incident forced its suspension.

"KEDO does not exist in a political vacuum and the submarine incident was a graphic reminder that our work program can be affected by events that take place outside KEDO and outside the KEDO relationship with North Korea," Bosworth said.

Bosworth told reporters he was encouraged by talks in New York last week between Washington, Seoul and Pyongyang on proposals for four-party talks including China to establish a new agreement to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

"I was pleased those talks went as well as could have been expected because KEDO does have a positive interest in seeing a meaningful dialogue develop between North and South Korea," he said. "That will make our work significantly easier if that dialogue occurs."
